\section{Reproducibility Details}
\label{app:reproducibility}

\paragraph{Fine-tuning configuration.}
All four fine-tuned models (Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on SciERC and DocRED) use identical LoRA hyperparameters: rank $r{=}16$, $\alpha{=}32$, dropout $0.05$, no bias, targeting all attention and MLP projection layers (\texttt{q\_proj}, \texttt{k\_proj}, \texttt{v\_proj}, \texttt{o\_proj}, \texttt{gate\_proj}, \texttt{up\_proj}, \texttt{down\_proj}).
Training uses AdamW with learning rate $2{\times}10^{-4}$, cosine schedule, warmup ratio $0.1$, effective batch size $16$, bf16 precision, gradient checkpointing, and completion-only loss for 3 epochs.
SciERC trains on 1,762 examples (260 dev) for 333 steps; DocRED trains on 3,053 examples (998 dev) for 573 steps.
Maximum sequence length is 2,048 (SciERC) and 4,096 (DocRED).
All runs use seed 42.

\paragraph{Hardware and software.}
Training runs on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPU (98\,GB VRAM).
SciERC fine-tuning takes approximately 11 minutes per model; DocRED takes approximately 1.5 hours.
Software versions: PyTorch 2.10, Transformers 4.57, PEFT 0.19, TRL 1.1, Accelerate 1.13.

\paragraph{Inference time.}
Table~\ref{tab:inference-time} reports per-document inference times for Qwen3-8B under zero-shot greedy decoding across constraint configurations.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\caption{Inference time (seconds/document, mean $\pm$ std) for Qwen3-8B, zero-shot, greedy decoding.}
\label{tab:inference-time}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lcc@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Configuration} & \textbf{SciERC} & \textbf{DocRED} \\
\midrule
Unconstrained       & $8.69 \pm 3.89$  & $19.75 \pm 8.99$  \\
Grammar-only        & $8.81 \pm 4.51$  & $20.58 \pm 10.75$ \\
Semantic-only       & $7.23 \pm 3.91$  & $20.53 \pm 9.37$  \\
Full S1             & $6.76 \pm 3.67$  & $20.39 \pm 9.43$  \\
Post-hoc            & $8.69 \pm 3.89$  & $19.78 \pm 8.99$  \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

On SciERC, full S1 constrained decoding is 22\% \emph{faster} than unconstrained generation because suppressing invalid tokens reduces output length.
On DocRED (longer documents), the masking computation adds a small constant overhead (+3.2\%) that slightly exceeds the token-savings effect.
Grammar-only and post-hoc filtering add negligible overhead ($<$4.2\% and $<$0.2\%, respectively).

1	\section{Beam Search Compatibility}
2	\label{app:beam-search}
3	
4	OntoCoDec's constraint enforcement is designed to be decoding-strategy agnostic.
5	The main experiments (\S\ref{sec:experiments}) use greedy decoding; Appendix~\ref{app:sampling} validates nucleus sampling.
6	Here we verify compatibility with beam search, completing coverage of the three standard decoding strategies.
7	
8	\paragraph{Implementation challenges.}
9	Two stateful components require adaptation for beam search.
10	(1)~The grammar layer (XGrammar) maintains an internal \texttt{GrammarMatcher} state that tracks the generated token sequence; beam reordering invalidates this state because beams are permuted across steps.
11	Our solution instantiates a fresh \texttt{GrammarMatcher} per beam per step and replays the beam's current token sequence through XGrammar's stateless accept API (64 lines of code).
12	(2)~The semantic layer's \texttt{TypeConstraintProcessor} accumulates entity and relation registries that assume a single generation path.
13	Our solution isolates state per beam by calling \texttt{detect()} on the full partial output at each step, reconstructing all entity/relation state from scratch for each beam independently (61 lines of code).
14	Both adaptations add ${\sim}125$ lines total without modifying the existing greedy/sampling logic.
15	
16	\paragraph{Results.}
17	Table~\ref{tab:beam-search} compares beam search ($k{=}4$, \texttt{early\_stopping=True}) against greedy decoding under full S1 constraints across six model-dataset combinations.
18	
19	\begin{table}[h]
20	\centering
21	\small
22	\caption{Beam search ($k{=}4$) vs.\ greedy decoding under full S1 constraints.
23	SciERC evaluated on full test set (551 documents); DocRED evaluated on matched 50-document subsets (same documents for greedy and beam).
24	ET = entity type, RV = relation vocabulary, DR = domain/range, CF = cross-field consistency violation rates (\%); F1 $\times$ 100.}
25	\label{tab:beam-search}
26	\begin{tabular}{@{}llcccccc@{}}
27	\toprule
28	\textbf{Model / Dataset} & \textbf{Decoding} & ET & RV & DR$\,\downarrow$ & CF$\,\downarrow$ & E-F1$\,\uparrow$ & R-F1$\,\uparrow$ \\
29	\midrule
30	\multirow{2}{*}{Qwen3-8B / SciERC (551)}
31	  & Greedy      & 0 & 0 & 0.93 & 9.90 & 30.98 & 8.36 \\
32	  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0.53} & 32.00 & 8.56 \\
33	\midrule
34	\multirow{2}{*}{Qwen3-8B / DocRED (50)}
35	  & Greedy      & 0 & 0 & 8.69 & 2.08 & 59.08 & 8.33 \\
36	  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0.55} & 58.64 & 9.37 \\
37	\midrule
38	\multirow{2}{*}{Llama-3.1-8B / SciERC (551)}
39	  & Greedy      & 0 & 0 & 0.08 & 6.56 & 23.49 & 2.54 \\
40	  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0.93} & 25.04 & 3.33 \\
41	\midrule
42	\multirow{2}{*}{Llama-3.1-8B / DocRED (50)}
43	  & Greedy      & 0 & 0 & 1.58 & 6.85 & 55.35 & 6.12 \\
44	  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0.94} & 55.62 & 9.47 \\
45	\midrule
46	\multirow{2}{*}{Mistral-7B / SciERC (551)}
47	  & Greedy      & 0 & 0 & 13.40 & 1.27 & 27.46 & 3.67 \\
48	  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & 13.79 & \textbf{0.57} & 26.66 & 4.37 \\
49	\midrule
50	\multirow{2}{*}{Mistral-7B / DocRED (50)}
51	  & Greedy      & 0 & 0 & 28.37 & 0.34 & 51.60 & 4.19 \\
52	  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & \textbf{21.37} & \textbf{0.19} & 51.78 & 5.70 \\
53	\bottomrule
54	\end{tabular}
55	\end{table}
56	
57	\paragraph{Discussion.}
58	For calibrated models (Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B), beam search achieves DR=0\% across all four model-dataset combinations (both SciERC with 7 entity types, 551 documents, and DocRED with 96 relation types, 50 documents), regardless of schema complexity.
59	On SciERC, beam search eliminates DR for both Qwen (0.93\%\,$\to$\,0\%) and Llama (0.08\%\,$\to$\,0\%), and substantially reduces CF (Qwen: 9.90\%\,$\to$\,0.53\%; Llama: 6.56\%\,$\to$\,0.93\%).
60	On DocRED (matched 50-document subsets), beam search eliminates DR for both Qwen (8.69\%\,$\to$\,0\%) and Llama (1.58\%\,$\to$\,0\%), with CF reductions of 74\% and 86\% respectively.
61	Llama DocRED shows the largest R-F1 gain ($+$3.4\,pp), consistent with beam search recovering valid type assignments that greedy decoding missed due to constraint fallback.
62	The CF reduction is an indirect effect: beam search reduces constraint-fallback frequency by exploring alternative token sequences that satisfy both grammar and semantic masks simultaneously, avoiding the fallback-to-grammar path that produces cross-field inconsistencies under greedy decoding.
63	
64	Mistral-7B-v0.3 constitutes a boundary condition on both datasets.
65	On SciERC (7 entity types), beam search does not reduce DR (13.4\%\,$\to$\,13.8\%), though CF drops by 55\% relative (1.27\%\,$\to$\,0.57\%) and R-F1 improves by $+$0.7\,pp; the unchanged DR confirms that all residual violations stem from entity type misclassification, not constraint-search failure.
66	On DocRED (96 relation types), beam search reduces DR by 25\% relative (28.4\%\,$\to$\,21.4\%): the more complex schema introduces constraint-search failures that beam exploration resolves, but the entity misclassification component remains.
67	This contrast reveals that beam search resolves constraint-search failure (where greedy decoding encounters grammar$\cap$semantic$=$\emptyset$ conflicts) but cannot overcome fundamental model calibration limitations in entity typing.
68	
69	\paragraph{Beam width ablation.}
70	Table~\ref{tab:beam-ablation} varies beam width $k \in \{1,2,4,8\}$ on Qwen3-8B / SciERC (551 documents) under full S1 constraints.
71	
72	\begin{table}[h]
73	\centering
74	\small
75	\caption{Effect of beam width on constraint satisfaction and extraction quality (Qwen3-8B, SciERC, 551 documents, full S1 constraints). $k{=}1$ corresponds to greedy decoding.}
76	\label{tab:beam-ablation}
77	\begin{tabular}{@{}rcccc@{}}
78	\toprule
79	$k$ & DR$\,\downarrow$ & CF$\,\downarrow$ & E-F1$\,\uparrow$ & R-F1$\,\uparrow$ \\
80	\midrule
81	1 (greedy) & 0.93 & 9.90 & 30.98 & 8.36 \\
82	2          & 0.35 & 4.12 & 31.54 & \textbf{8.75} \\
83	4          & \textbf{0}    & 0.53 & 32.00 & 8.56 \\
84	8          & \textbf{0}    & \textbf{0.08} & \textbf{32.18} & 8.39 \\
85	\bottomrule
86	\end{tabular}
87	\end{table}
88	
89	DR elimination at $k{\geq}4$ confirms that constraint-search failure is resolved with moderate exploration width.
90	CF continues to decrease with larger beam (0.08\% at $k{=}8$, only 2 residual violations), while entity extraction quality improves monotonically.
91	$k{=}4$ represents the optimal cost-effectiveness trade-off: it eliminates all DR violations at roughly half the compute cost of $k{=}8$.
92	
93	\paragraph{Composability with fine-tuning.}

\section{Beam Search Compatibility}
\label{app:beam-search}

OntoCoDec's constraint enforcement is designed to be decoding-strategy agnostic.
The main experiments (\S\ref{sec:experiments}) use greedy decoding; Appendix~\ref{app:sampling} validates nucleus sampling.
Here we verify compatibility with beam search, completing coverage of the three standard decoding strategies.

\paragraph{Implementation challenges.}
Two stateful components require adaptation for beam search.
(1)~The grammar layer (XGrammar) maintains an internal \texttt{GrammarMatcher} state that tracks the generated token sequence; beam reordering invalidates this state because beams are permuted across steps.
Our solution instantiates a fresh \texttt{GrammarMatcher} per beam per step and replays the beam's current token sequence through XGrammar's stateless accept API (64 lines of code).
(2)~The semantic layer's \texttt{TypeConstraintProcessor} accumulates entity and relation registries that assume a single generation path.
Our solution isolates state per beam by calling \texttt{detect()} on the full partial output at each step, reconstructing all entity/relation state from scratch for each beam independently (61 lines of code).
Both adaptations add ${\sim}125$ lines total without modifying the existing greedy/sampling logic.

\paragraph{Results.}
Table~\ref{tab:beam-search} compares beam search ($k{=}4$, \texttt{early\_stopping=True}) against greedy decoding under full S1 constraints across six model-dataset combinations.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\caption{Beam search ($k{=}4$) vs.\ greedy decoding under full S1 constraints.
SciERC evaluated on full test set (551 documents); DocRED evaluated on matched 50-document subsets (same documents for greedy and beam).
ET = entity type, RV = relation vocabulary, DR = domain/range, CF = cross-field consistency violation rates (\%); F1 $\times$ 100.}
\label{tab:beam-search}
\begin{tabular}{@{}llcccccc@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Model / Dataset} & \textbf{Decoding} & ET & RV & DR$\,\downarrow$ & CF$\,\downarrow$ & E-F1$\,\uparrow$ & R-F1$\,\uparrow$ \\
\midrule
\multirow{2}{*}{Qwen3-8B / SciERC (551)}
  & Greedy      & 0 & 0 & 0.93 & 9.90 & 30.98 & 8.36 \\
  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0.53} & 32.00 & 8.56 \\
\midrule
\multirow{2}{*}{Qwen3-8B / DocRED (50)}
  & Greedy      & 0 & 0 & 8.69 & 2.08 & 59.08 & 8.33 \\
  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0.55} & 58.64 & 9.37 \\
\midrule
\multirow{2}{*}{Llama-3.1-8B / SciERC (551)}
  & Greedy      & 0 & 0 & 0.08 & 6.56 & 23.49 & 2.54 \\
  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0.93} & 25.04 & 3.33 \\
\midrule
\multirow{2}{*}{Llama-3.1-8B / DocRED (50)}
  & Greedy      & 0 & 0 & 1.58 & 6.85 & 55.35 & 6.12 \\
  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0.94} & 55.62 & 9.47 \\
\midrule
\multirow{2}{*}{Mistral-7B / SciERC (551)}
  & Greedy      & 0 & 0 & 13.40 & 1.27 & 27.46 & 3.67 \\
  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & 13.79 & \textbf{0.57} & 26.66 & 4.37 \\
\midrule
\multirow{2}{*}{Mistral-7B / DocRED (50)}
  & Greedy      & 0 & 0 & 28.37 & 0.34 & 51.60 & 4.19 \\
  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & \textbf{21.37} & \textbf{0.19} & 51.78 & 5.70 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Discussion.}
For calibrated models (Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B), beam search achieves DR=0\% across all four model-dataset combinations (both SciERC with 7 entity types, 551 documents, and DocRED with 96 relation types, 50 documents), regardless of schema complexity.
On SciERC, beam search eliminates DR for both Qwen (0.93\%\,$\to$\,0\%) and Llama (0.08\%\,$\to$\,0\%), and substantially reduces CF (Qwen: 9.90\%\,$\to$\,0.53\%; Llama: 6.56\%\,$\to$\,0.93\%).
On DocRED (matched 50-document subsets), beam search eliminates DR for both Qwen (8.69\%\,$\to$\,0\%) and Llama (1.58\%\,$\to$\,0\%), with CF reductions of 74\% and 86\% respectively.
Llama DocRED shows the largest R-F1 gain ($+$3.4\,pp), consistent with beam search recovering valid type assignments that greedy decoding missed due to constraint fallback.
The CF reduction is an indirect effect: beam search reduces constraint-fallback frequency by exploring alternative token sequences that satisfy both grammar and semantic masks simultaneously, avoiding the fallback-to-grammar path that produces cross-field inconsistencies under greedy decoding.

Mistral-7B-v0.3 constitutes a boundary condition on both datasets.
On SciERC (7 entity types), beam search does not reduce DR (13.4\%\,$\to$\,13.8\%), though CF drops by 55\% relative (1.27\%\,$\to$\,0.57\%) and R-F1 improves by $+$0.7\,pp; the unchanged DR confirms that all residual violations stem from entity type misclassification, not constraint-search failure.
On DocRED (96 relation types), beam search reduces DR by 25\% relative (28.4\%\,$\to$\,21.4\%): the more complex schema introduces constraint-search failures that beam exploration resolves, but the entity misclassification component remains.
This contrast reveals that beam search resolves constraint-search failure (where greedy decoding encounters grammar$\cap$semantic$=$\emptyset$ conflicts) but cannot overcome fundamental model calibration limitations in entity typing.

\paragraph{Beam width ablation.}
Table~\ref{tab:beam-ablation} varies beam width $k \in \{1,2,4,8\}$ on Qwen3-8B / SciERC (551 documents) under full S1 constraints.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\caption{Effect of beam width on constraint satisfaction and extraction quality (Qwen3-8B, SciERC, 551 documents, full S1 constraints). $k{=}1$ corresponds to greedy decoding.}
\label{tab:beam-ablation}
\begin{tabular}{@{}rcccc@{}}
\toprule
$k$ & DR$\,\downarrow$ & CF$\,\downarrow$ & E-F1$\,\uparrow$ & R-F1$\,\uparrow$ \\
\midrule
1 (greedy) & 0.93 & 9.90 & 30.98 & 8.36 \\
2          & 0.35 & 4.12 & 31.54 & \textbf{8.75} \\
4          & \textbf{0}    & 0.53 & 32.00 & 8.56 \\
8          & \textbf{0}    & \textbf{0.08} & \textbf{32.18} & 8.39 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

DR elimination at $k{\geq}4$ confirms that constraint-search failure is resolved with moderate exploration width.
CF continues to decrease with larger beam (0.08\% at $k{=}8$, only 2 residual violations), while entity extraction quality improves monotonically.
$k{=}4$ represents the optimal cost-effectiveness trade-off: it eliminates all DR violations at roughly half the compute cost of $k{=}8$.

\paragraph{Composability with fine-tuning.}
Under greedy decoding, the fine-tuned Qwen3-8B (LoRA, SciERC) with full S1 constraints already achieves DR=0\% but retains CF=1.18\% (21 cross-field violations across 551 documents), with E-F1=67.05 and R-F1=43.77.
Adding beam search ($k{=}4$) eliminates all residual CF violations (1.18\%\,$\to$\,0\%), yielding zero violations across all four metrics (ET=0\%, RV=0\%, DR=0\%, CF=0\%) while preserving extraction quality (E-F1=66.88, R-F1=44.23; changes within $\pm$0.5\,pp).
This confirms that the three constraint mechanisms (grammar masking, semantic domain-range filtering, and beam exploration) are fully composable: each addresses a distinct violation source without interfering with the others or degrading task performance.

Beam search on DocRED introduces a modest increase in parse failures (3/50, 6\%) compared to greedy (1.1\%), as longer beam-generated sequences occasionally produce malformed JSON in complex documents.
Wall-clock overhead is modest; \texttt{early\_stopping} terminates generation once all beams produce a complete sequence, limiting the additional compute to partial-sequence exploration rather than full-length replication.
Combined with the sampling robustness results (Appendix~\ref{app:sampling}), these findings confirm that OntoCoDec's constraint enforcement is compatible with greedy, sampling, and beam search decoding without modification to the core constraint logic.

We also explored a type-consensus constraint that forces identical entity types across all relations within a document.
However, CF violations occur precisely where the consensus type conflicts with domain-range constraints, creating a fundamental CF$\leftrightarrow$DR trade-off.
With DR-aware enforcement (skipping consensus when it would violate domain-range), the layer becomes a no-op (100\% skip rate on 551 SciERC documents and 50 DocRED documents).
This confirms that beam search resolves the CF$\leftrightarrow$DR tension through a fundamentally different mechanism: token-level exploration of paths satisfying both constraints simultaneously.

\begin{abstract}
We present \textsc{OntoCoDec}, which compiles Information Extraction (IE) ontology schemas into two composable token-level decoding constraints that provide formal guarantees during autoregressive generation:
(1)~a \emph{grammar layer} (XGrammar context-free grammar) guaranteeing JSON structural validity and entity/relation vocabulary membership (eliminating entity type and relation vocabulary violations); and
(2)~a \emph{semantic layer} guaranteeing per-triple domain/range type compliance via a stateful entity registry and dynamic logit masking.
The two layers compose via bitwise AND on logit masks, with the grammar layer as an enabling prerequisite.
%
Without constraints, Large Language Model (LLM) based IE produces systematic domain/range (DR) violations: 15.37\% on SciERC (7 relations) and 18.46\% on DocRED (96 relations), comparable rates governed by \emph{constraint tightness} rather than ontology scale.
\textsc{OntoCoDec} reduces DR by 42--99\% across three model families (Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B) with no significant F1 cost.
For the primary model (Qwen3-8B): SciERC $+$0.13\,pp ($p{=}0.58$), DocRED $+$0.50\,pp ($p{<}0.001$); other models show comparable or larger gains (\S\ref{sec:cross-model}).
% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_full_s1, phase2_docred_full_s1, llama_docred_full_s1, mistral_docred
Residual DR correlates with the product of schema tightness and baseline violation rate: for calibrated models (Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B), the dual-factor pattern explains nearly all variance ($R^2{=}0.99$, $n{=}4$), while Mistral's higher entity misclassification rate places it outside this regime (Appendix~\ref{app:dual-factor}).
Composed with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning, DR reaches $\leq$\,0.09\% (SciERC) and 0.20\% (DocRED) with R-F1 within $\pm$0.6\,pp, confirming orthogonal composability.
Per-relation independent enforcement introduces a cross-field consistency (CF) vs.\ DR trade-off: CF violations arise (up to 12\% in zero-shot) as the cost of per-slot domain/range guarantees; fine-tuning resolves this tension (CF\,$\leq$\,1.2\%).
\end{abstract}

4	\paragraph{Grammar-Constrained Decoding.}
5	XGrammar~\cite{dong2025xgrammar}, Outlines~\cite{willard2023outlines}, LMQL~\cite{beurer-kellner2023lmql}, DOMINO~\cite{beurer-kellner2024domino}, SynCode~\cite{ugare2024syncode}, and ASAp~\cite{park2024grammar} ensure every token belongs to a grammar-valid continuation; IterGen~\cite{ugare2025itergen} adds backtracking.
6	These guarantee format validity but cannot enforce cross-field semantic constraints such as ontology domain/range rules.
7	
8	\paragraph{Semantic Constrained Decoding for Code.}
9	Synchromesh~\cite{synchromesh_iclr2022}, PICARD~\cite{scholak2021picard}, MGD~\cite{mgd_neurips2023}, and \citet{pldi2025_type_constrained_codegen} enforce type and scope constraints in code generation; OntoCoDec migrates this paradigm to IE.
10	
11	\paragraph{Vocabulary and Type-Constrained Generation.}
12	\citet{roth_yih_2004} establish relational type compatibility as a hard constraint via ILP, though applied post-hoc.
13	GENRE~\cite{decao2021genre}, AdaKGC~\cite{adakgc_emnlp2023}, GCD~\cite{geng2023gcd}, and GoLLIE~\cite{sainz2024gollie} constrain \emph{which tokens} can appear but not \emph{which type combinations} are valid per relation; GCD's per-position trie enforces vocabulary membership (equivalent to our grammar layer) but cannot capture the conditional dependency between head and tail types that our semantic layer provides.
14	DORE~\cite{vukovic2024dore} enforces ontological consistency via chain-of-thought output selection with confidence thresholds, a generate-then-select paradigm distinct from OntoCoDec's token-level logit masking during generation.
15	GenIE~\cite{josifoski2022genie} constrains entity generation to a candidate trie but does not enforce relation-specific type constraints.
16	EnriCo~\cite{zaratiana2024enrico} applies ASP constraints during decoding for joint entity-relation extraction, a hard-constraint approach like ours but with task-specific manually authored rules rather than ontology-compiled masks.
17	Training-based methods~\cite{paolini2021tanl,cabot2021rebel,lu2022uie,knowcoder_acl2024,li2023codeie} and span-based models such as GLiNER~\cite{zaratiana2023gliner} encode IE structure via training or architecture but provide only \emph{soft} guidance.
18	Post-hoc approaches~\cite{khorshidi2025odke,spires_2024,ontologx_2025} validate outputs against ontologies after generation; OntoCoDec \emph{prevents} violations during decoding.
19	
20	\paragraph{Quality Impact of Constrained Decoding.}
21	CRANE~\cite{banerjee2025crane} and \citet{schall2025hiddencost} show grammar restrictions can degrade reasoning, but \citet{tam2024letmespeak} find extraction-style tasks are robust to (or benefit from) constraints.
22	BoostCD~\cite{sakota2025boostcd} combines constrained and unconstrained outputs via boosting for IE, complementing our decoding-time approach with a training-time strategy.
23	OntoCoDec confirms extraction robustness: violations decrease by 42--99\% with zero F1 degradation across three model families (extended survey in Appendix~\ref{app:related_work}).

% Section 1: Introduction (compressed, 669→~550 words)

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large language models are increasingly deployed for zero-shot information extraction~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity is guaranteed to carry a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.
We call such outputs \emph{domain/range violations}: structurally valid triples that are ontologically invalid.
In a systematic study, we find violations are pervasive: 15.4\% of triples on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} and 18.5\% on DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred}, driven by \emph{constraint tightness} (few valid type pairs per relation) rather than ontology scale.
Relations with tight constraints exhibit far higher rates (\textsc{Compare}: 42.4\%) than loosely constrained ones (\textsc{Used-for}: 0.8\%).

Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on average but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).
Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} guarantees syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
Post-hoc filtering achieves higher F1 in most zero-shot settings via precision gains, but at the cost of discarding up to 48\% of predictions including true positives; at high rejection rates (e.g., Mistral DocRED 73.7\%), it discards the majority of outputs, making it impractical.
OntoCoDec preserves recall by enforcing constraints during generation rather than discarding non-compliant outputs.
Training-based approaches~\cite{sainz2024gollie,lu2022uie} provide only soft guidance that cannot eliminate violations.

We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec} (\textbf{Onto}logy-\textbf{Co}mpiled \textbf{Dec}oding), a framework that compiles an IE ontology into two composable layers of decoding-time constraints.
The \emph{grammar layer} enforces JSON well-formedness and vocabulary validity via XGrammar.
The \emph{semantic layer} maintains a stateful entity registry during generation: as entities are decoded, the registry records type assignments; when relation arguments are generated, dynamic logit masking restricts output to types compatible with the relation's domain/range specification.
The layers compose via bitwise AND with an \emph{enabling dependency}: the grammar layer guarantees vocabulary membership, enabling the semantic layer to look up domain/range rules.
On SciERC, OntoCoDec reduces DR violations from 15.37\% to 0.93\% ($\downarrow$94\%) while remaining F1-neutral ($+$0.13\,pp).

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item The first systematic study of ontological constraint violations in LLM-based IE (spanning per-relation tightness analysis, dual-factor characterization, and post-hoc baseline comparison), showing that violation rates are driven by constraint tightness rather than ontology size, and that prompt-level intervention is per-relation unreliable.
    \item OntoCoDec, a two-layer compiled constraint framework that is the first to enforce pair-based domain/range type constraints via compiled stateful logit masks during autoregressive IE.
    Unlike type-constrained decoding in code generation, where output types are statically determined by the grammar, IE requires stateful cross-field constraints because entity type validity depends on the co-occurring relation within each triple.
    \item Empirical validation on 3 models $\times$ 2 datasets: DR $\downarrow$76--99\% on SciERC and $\downarrow$42--90\% across three models on DocRED, with significant R-F1 gains on DocRED (Qwen $p{<}0.001$, Llama $p{=}0.013$), model-agnostic structural guarantees, composability with fine-tuning (DR\,$\leq$\,0.20\% at $<$0.6\,pp F1 cost), and characterization of the CF$\leftrightarrow$DR trade-off inherent to per-relation enforcement (resolved by fine-tuning to CF\,$\leq$\,1.2\%).
\end{enumerate}

- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).
TRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`; user asks for the Claude API, Anthropic SDK, or Managed Agents; user adds/modifies/tunes a Claude feature (caching, thinking, compaction, tool use, batch, files, citations, memory) or model (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku) in a file; questions about prompt caching / cache hit rate in an Anthropic SDK project.
SKIP: file imports `openai`/other-provider SDK, filename like `*-openai.py`/`*-generic.py`, provider-neutral code, general programming/ML.
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a pull request
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch
